raw_text:
Cardiac amyloidosis is an infiltrative cardiomyopathy caused by extracellular myocardial deposition of misfolded amyloid fibrils. The clinically dominant forms are immunoglobulin light-chain (AL) amyloidosis, a plasma-cell dyscrasia with rapidly progressive toxicity, and transthyretin amyloidosis (ATTR), which is either hereditary (ATTRv) or wild-type (ATTRwt) [1,2]. Pathologic typing is essential because prognosis and treatment differ fundamentally; mass-spectrometry proteomics has largely superseded morphology alone when tissue is available [3].

Recognition has improved because cardiac amyloidosis is no longer considered rare. Monoclonal gammopathy is common in older adults, complicating interpretation of screening tests [4]. ATTRwt is frequent at autopsy in the very elderly [5], is found in a subset of heart failure with preserved ejection fraction [6,7], and coexists with severe aortic stenosis in older patients undergoing valve intervention [8]. ATTRv is influenced by genotype and ancestry; the Val122Ile variant, enriched among individuals of African ancestry, is an important cause of late-onset cardiomyopathy [9]. Contemporary reviews emphasize that ATTR-CM often presents after years of “hypertensive” remodeling, carpal tunnel syndrome, spinal stenosis, neuropathy, or autonomic symptoms [10].

Clinically, patients develop exertional intolerance, congestion, atrial arrhythmias, conduction disease, and relatively low blood pressure despite increased ventricular wall thickness. Echocardiography typically shows concentric thickening, biatrial enlargement, restrictive filling, valve thickening, pericardial effusion, and reduced longitudinal strain with relative apical sparing [11]. Cardiac magnetic resonance adds tissue characterization: native T1 and extracellular volume are elevated [12], while diffuse subendocardial or transmural late gadolinium enhancement carries prognostic value [13]. Bone-avid tracer scintigraphy transformed diagnosis: grade 2–3 myocardial uptake with technetium-labeled tracers strongly supports ATTR, but only after AL amyloidosis is excluded with serum free light chains plus serum and urine immunofixation [14-16]. Fat-pad biopsy is useful in AL but has lower sensitivity in ATTRwt, so negative extracardiac biopsy does not exclude cardiac disease [17,18].

Risk stratification is biomarker-driven. In AL amyloidosis, troponin and NT-proBNP identify cardiac involvement and stage prognosis, with serum free light-chain burden refining risk [19,20]. In ATTR-CM, natriuretic peptide, renal function, and troponin-based systems identify patients with markedly different survival, supporting early diagnosis before advanced low-output disease develops [21,22].

Management combines disease-modifying therapy with careful heart-failure care. Loop diuretics are the cornerstone for congestion; neurohormonal agents used for conventional heart failure are often poorly tolerated because of autonomic dysfunction, restrictive physiology, renal impairment, or hypotension. Atrial fibrillation is common, may be poorly tolerated, and warrants a low threshold for anticoagulation because intracardiac thrombus can occur even with modest arrhythmia burden [23,24]. Pacemakers are used for symptomatic bradyarrhythmias, whereas defibrillator benefit is less certain because electromechanical dissociation and progressive pump failure are common modes of death.

In AL amyloidosis, treatment urgency is high: hematologic response must be achieved quickly to reduce light-chain cardiotoxicity. High-dose melphalan with autologous transplantation can be effective only in highly selected patients; randomized data highlighted the danger of treatment-related mortality in advanced disease [25]. Daratumumab added to cyclophosphamide, bortezomib, and dexamethasone has become a major advance, producing deeper hematologic and organ responses [26]. In ATTR-CM, tafamidis, a transthyretin stabilizer, reduced mortality and cardiovascular hospitalization in a pivotal trial [27]. Diflunisal also stabilizes transthyretin but is limited by renal, fluid-retention, and gastrointestinal toxicity [28]. Gene-silencing therapies such as patisiran improve neuropathy and show favorable cardiac biomarker and structural signals in ATTRv disease [29], while in-vivo CRISPR-Cas9 editing has demonstrated profound transthyretin reduction, raising the possibility of one-time therapy [30]. Overall, the field is moving from late recognition and palliation toward genotype-aware, mechanism-based treatment initiated earlier in the disease course.
